systems.name: Spring and Autumn
systems.summary: A period of rivalry among regional states under the declining Zhou royal order.
systems.dateNote: 770–481 BCE is a supported scholarly convention. This is a historical period, not a regime; alternatives use 479, 476, or 475 as endpoint.

systems.name: Warring States
systems.summary: An era of competing territorial states, ending with Qin's conquests in 221 BCE.
systems.dateNote: 481–221 BCE is an explicit Met chronology, not an error to 'fix' solely because another chronology uses 475 or 403. It is periodization rather than a single founding event.

systems.name: Qin-Han system
systems.summary: An umbrella period for Qin and Han imperial rule and their intervening transitions.
systems.dateNote: 221 BCE–220 CE is an editorial umbrella for Qin and Han, including intervening conflicts and Xin; not one continuous regime. Stored duration 441 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years are 440 because BCE/CE has no year zero.

systems.name: Sui-Tang
systems.dateNote: 581–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

systems.name: Modern China
systems.dateNote: 1912–2026 is an editorial exhibition frame. Modern China has no universally agreed beginning; 2026 is a display horizon.

systems.name: Song multi-state system
systems.summary: Multi-state balance between Song, Liao, Jin, and Western Xia
systems.dateNote: 960–1279 follows the Song dynasty as an editorial frame for changing concurrent states. The named states did not all coexist throughout the interval, and this aggregate does not assert Song sovereignty over them.

systems.name: Sixteen Kingdoms
systems.summary: A period of rival states, chiefly in northern China, alongside the Jin courts; Northern Wei unified the north in 439.

systems.name: Northern and Southern Dynasties
systems.summary: Successive southern courts and rival northern dynasties coexisted until Sui conquered Chen in 589.
systems.dateNote: 420–589 is a supported periodization; Northern Wei began earlier, in 386. Do not infer containment of all northern states.

systems.name: Five Dynasties
systems.summary: Five successive dynasties held the northern imperial succession between Tang and Song.
systems.dateNote: 907–960 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

systems.name: Ten Kingdoms
systems.summary: Regional states coexisted with the Five Dynasties and early Song, with Northern Han the last to fall in 979.
systems.dateNote: 902–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

regimes.name: Xia
regimes.summary: Traditional dynasty; its dates and identification with archaeological remains are debated.
regimes.dateNote: 2070–1600 BCE is one modern reconstructed chronology, not securely established exact dates. Xia's identification with excavated cultures and the historical status of its early rulers remain debated. Display as approximate/traditional.

regimes.name: Shang
regimes.summary: The earliest Chinese dynasty securely documented by contemporary inscriptions, especially those from late Shang Anyang.
regimes.dateNote: Museum chronology supports approximately 1600–1046 BCE; early boundaries are reconstructions. 'First archaeological state' is misleading because earlier complex societies are archaeologically known.

regimes.name: Zhou
regimes.summary: Zhou rule is conventionally divided into Western and Eastern phases.
regimes.dateNote: Approximately 1046–256 BCE follows the Met chronology. The beginning is reconstructed; 256 BCE is the conventional end of Zhou royal rule.

regimes.name: Western Zhou
regimes.summary: The early Zhou royal order, before the court's eastward relocation.
regimes.dateNote: Approximately 1046–771 BCE follows the Met. The reconstructed start should not be presented as unquestionably exact.

regimes.name: Eastern Zhou
regimes.summary: The Zhou court ruled from the east while regional states increasingly exercised independent power.
regimes.dateNote: 770–256 BCE: 770 marks King Ping's move to Luoyi; 256 is the conventional end of the Zhou royal house. Warring States continues beyond this dynasty's end.

regimes.name: Qin
regimes.summary: The Qin imperial dynasty followed the conquest of the rival states in 221 BCE.
regimes.dateNote: 221–206 BCE is the standard museum range for the imperial Qin dynasty, not the longer history of the Qin state.

regimes.name: Western Han
regimes.summary: The first phase of Han rule, conventionally dated from Liu Bang's kingship in 206 BCE; he became emperor in 202 BCE.
regimes.dateNote: 206 BCE–9 CE is the standard museum convention, beginning with Liu Bang's kingship; 202 BCE marks his imperial accession and is used by other historians. Duration 215 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years 214.

regimes.name: Xin
regimes.summary: Wang Mang's Xin dynasty interrupted Han rule from 9 to 23 CE.
regimes.dateNote: 9–23 CE follows the Cambridge History of China chronology for Wang Mang's dynasty.

regimes.name: Eastern Han
regimes.summary: The restored Han dynasty, conventionally dated 25–220 CE.
regimes.dateNote: 25–220 CE follows the Met chronology; restoration in 25 is distinct from the earlier Gengshi claimant 23–25.

regimes.name: Wei
regimes.summary: Northern state
regimes.dateNote: 220–265 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Shu
regimes.summary: Han claimant
regimes.dateNote: 221–263 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Wu
regimes.summary: Southern state
regimes.dateNote: 222–280 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Western Jin
regimes.summary: Short reunification
regimes.dateNote: 266–316 is supported with calendrical qualification: Cambridge explicitly gives 265 or 266 for the foundation. Retain 266.

regimes.name: Sui
regimes.summary: Reunifies China
regimes.dateNote: 581–618 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

regimes.name: Tang
regimes.summary: Imperial peak
regimes.dateNote: 618–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

regimes.name: Republic of China (mainland period)
regimes.summary: Republican state on mainland China before 1949
regimes.dateNote: 1 January 1912 is the republic’s founding. 1949 ends this mainland-period card, not the existence of the ROC government, which relocated to Taiwan. Qing abdication followed on 12 February 1912.

regimes.name: People's Republic of China
regimes.summary: Modern Chinese state founded in 1949
regimes.dateNote: Proclaimed 1 October 1949. 2026 is the dataset display horizon, not an end date.

regimes.name: Northern Song
regimes.summary: Reunifies much of China
regimes.dateNote: 960–1127 is the standard Northern Song chronology.

regimes.name: Southern Song
regimes.summary: Southern continuation after loss of north
regimes.dateNote: 1127–1279 is the standard Southern Song chronology; 1127 does not mean the court immediately settled permanently at Hangzhou.

regimes.name: Liao (Khitan)
regimes.summary: Steppe empire controlling north China
regimes.dateNote: 907–1125 is a supported Khitan-state convention; 916 denotes imperial proclamation. Name already qualifies Liao as Khitan.

regimes.name: Western Xia
regimes.summary: Tangut state in northwest
regimes.dateNote: 1038 dates imperial proclamation by Li Yuanhao; Tangut power predates it. UNESCO's reviewed chronology supports 1038–1227.

regimes.name: Jin (Jurchen)
regimes.summary: Conquers northern Song and dominates north China
regimes.dateNote: 1115–1234 dates the Jurchen Jin; distinct from the earlier Jin (晋).

regimes.name: Yuan
regimes.summary: Mongol dynasty ruling China
regimes.dateNote: 1271 dates the Yuan dynastic name, 1279 the final Song conquest. 1368 ends Yuan rule from Beijing, not all subsequent Mongol or Northern Yuan rule.

regimes.name: Ming
regimes.summary: Restoration of Han Chinese rule after Yuan
regimes.dateNote: 1368–1644 is the main Ming court convention. Southern Ming successors survived after Beijing fell.

regimes.name: Qing
regimes.summary: Manchu dynasty ruling a multiethnic empire
regimes.dateNote: 1644–1912 is valid for rule from Beijing. The Qing dynastic name was proclaimed in 1636; the emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, after the revolution began in 1911.

regimes.name: Eastern Jin
regimes.summary: The Jin court continued in southern China at Jiankang after losing the north, alongside rival northern states.
regimes.dateNote: 317–420 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Han Zhao (Former Zhao)
regimes.summary: Founded as Han, this state later adopted the name Zhao; its armies captured the Western Jin capitals.
regimes.dateNote: 304–329 includes the Han phase; Former Zhao naming begins 319. Retain combined label.

regimes.name: Later Zhao
regimes.summary: Shi Le founded a rival Zhao state that became a major power in northern China.
regimes.dateNote: Cambridge History table confirms 319–351; EMC thesaurus gives a different 352 endpoint.

regimes.name: Former Yan
regimes.summary: The Murong Xianbei founded this northern state, which expanded into the Central Plain before conquest by Former Qin.
regimes.dateNote: 337–370 is the China Institute/Liaoning archaeology exhibition chronology; 337 is royal proclamation.

regimes.name: Former Qin
regimes.summary: Former Qin briefly unified northern China; defeat by Eastern Jin at the Fei River in 383 precipitated its fragmentation.
regimes.dateNote: 351–394 agrees with EMC scholarly thesaurus. Other tables differ; retain conventional terminal remnant date.

regimes.name: Later Qin
regimes.summary: A Qiang-led state based at Chang'an, Later Qin supported Buddhist translation before conquest by Eastern Jin.
regimes.dateNote: 384–417 agrees with scholarly thesaurus.

regimes.name: Liu Song
regimes.summary: Liu Yu replaced Eastern Jin, founding the first of the four Southern Dynasties.
regimes.dateNote: 420–479 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Southern Qi
regimes.summary: The Xiao family's short-lived dynasty succeeded Liu Song in southern China.
regimes.dateNote: 479–502 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Liang
regimes.summary: A southern dynasty based at Jiankang, remembered for court culture and Buddhist patronage.
regimes.dateNote: 502–557 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Chen
regimes.summary: The last Southern Dynasty ruled from Jiankang until Sui conquered it in 589.
regimes.dateNote: 557–589 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Northern Wei
regimes.summary: Founded by the Tuoba Xianbei, Northern Wei unified the north in 439 before dividing into eastern and western successors.
regimes.dateNote: 386–534 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Eastern Wei
regimes.summary: The eastern successor to Northern Wei governed from Ye before replacement by Northern Qi.
regimes.dateNote: 534–550 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Western Wei
regimes.summary: The western successor to Northern Wei ruled from Chang'an before Northern Zhou replaced it.
regimes.dateNote: 535–557 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Northern Qi
regimes.summary: Northern Qi succeeded Eastern Wei and competed with Northern Zhou, which conquered it in 577.
regimes.dateNote: 550–577 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Northern Zhou
regimes.summary: Northern Zhou replaced Western Wei, conquered Northern Qi in 577, and gave way to Sui in 581.
regimes.dateNote: 557–581 follows the museum chronology.

regimes.name: Later Liang
regimes.summary: Zhu Wen replaced Tang with Later Liang, the first of five successive northern dynasties.
regimes.dateNote: 907–923 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

regimes.name: Later Tang
regimes.summary: Li Cunxu established this Shatuo-led dynasty after overthrowing Later Liang.
regimes.dateNote: 923–936 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

regimes.name: Later Jin
regimes.summary: Shi Jingtang founded Later Jin with Khitan support; a later Khitan invasion ended the dynasty.
regimes.dateNote: Cambridge journal explicitly supports the existing endpoints; older tables give one-year-earlier terminal years.

regimes.name: Later Han
regimes.summary: Liu Zhiyuan founded this short-lived northern dynasty after the fall of Later Jin.
regimes.dateNote: Cambridge journal explicitly supports the existing endpoints; older tables give one-year-earlier terminal years.

regimes.name: Later Zhou
regimes.summary: The last of the Five Dynasties strengthened the northern state before Zhao Kuangyin founded Song.
regimes.dateNote: 951–960 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

regimes.name: Wu (Yang Wu)
regimes.summary: Based in the lower Yangtze region, Wu grew from late-Tang regional rule and was replaced by Southern Tang.
regimes.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

regimes.name: Former Shu
regimes.summary: Wang Jian founded an independent state in Sichuan; Later Tang conquered it in 925.
regimes.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

regimes.name: Wuyue
regimes.summary: The Qian family's coastal kingdom in the Zhejiang region endured until its submission to Song in 978.
regimes.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

regimes.name: Chu (Ma Chu)
regimes.summary: The Ma family ruled this Hunan-based kingdom until Southern Tang intervention ended the dynasty.
regimes.dateNote: 907–951 is supported by Kurz; 927 is the later kingdom milestone used in other tables. Retain broad state span.

regimes.name: Min
regimes.summary: The Wang family's Fujian-based kingdom fragmented through internal conflict before its collapse.
regimes.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

regimes.name: Southern Han
regimes.summary: Based at Guangzhou, this southern kingdom was founded as Yue and renamed Han before eventual Song conquest.
regimes.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

regimes.name: Jingnan (Nanping)
regimes.summary: A small kingdom around Jingzhou on the middle Yangtze, Jingnan survived between larger neighbors until Song conquest.
regimes.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

regimes.name: Later Shu
regimes.summary: The Meng family restored an independent Sichuan kingdom after Former Shu; Song conquered it in 965.
regimes.dateNote: 934–965 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

regimes.name: Southern Tang
regimes.summary: Southern Tang replaced Wu in the lower Yangtze and fostered an influential court culture before Song conquest.
regimes.dateNote: 937–975 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

regimes.name: Northern Han
regimes.summary: Based at Taiyuan, this northern member of the Ten Kingdoms survived with Khitan support until Song conquered it.
regimes.dateNote: 951–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

events.name: Yu founds Xia (legendary tradition)
events.summary: Later tradition credits the culture hero Yu with founding Xia; neither the act nor its year is independently established.
events.dateNote: No historically verified founding year. Existing 2070 BCE derives from the selected Xia reconstruction, not independent evidence of Yu founding a dynasty. Do not display it as an exact dated event. Numeric year is retained solely as an editorial placement for compatibility; it is not an asserted historical date.

events.name: Oracle-bone writing (c. 1200 BCE)
events.summary: Late-Shang oracle-bone inscriptions preserve the earliest substantial surviving body of Chinese writing.
events.dateNote: 1200 BCE is an approximate representative date for surviving late-Shang inscriptions, not a dated invention of writing. The claim is earliest surviving substantial Chinese writing, not earliest writing worldwide.

events.name: Zhou conquest of Shang
events.summary: The Zhou defeated Shang around 1046 BCE, according to a widely used modern chronology.
events.dateNote: 1046 BCE is a widely adopted reconstructed date for the Zhou conquest, not universally agreed. Display c. 1046 BCE.

events.name: Qin unification
events.summary: Qin completed its conquest of the rival states and established an empire in 221 BCE.
events.dateNote: 221 BCE marks completion of the conquests and formation of imperial Qin.

events.name: Qin standardizes weights and measures
events.summary: Qin's First Emperor ordered a common system of weights and measures across the empire in 221 BCE.
events.dateNote: The specific weights-and-measures edict is dated 221 BCE, not 220. Other standardization measures were a process; narrowing the label provides a defensible single year.

events.name: Han court establishes Five Classics patronage
events.summary: The Han court promoted study of the Five Classics in 136 BCE, an important stage in the growth of state-sponsored classical learning.
events.dateNote: 130 BCE has no specific event support.136 BCE is a documented milestone in official promotion of the Five Classics. Formation of state Confucianism was gradual, not a single adoption event.

events.name: Zhang Qian's first western mission
events.summary: Zhang Qian departed on a western mission conventionally dated 138 BCE, helping expand Han knowledge of Central Asia.
events.dateNote: 130 BCE is unsupported as a precise 'Silk Road expansion' event.138 BCE dates Zhang Qian's departure in the UNESCO education publication; another UNESCO overview uses 139 BCE. Trade routes predated and developed after this mission.

events.name: Buddhism reaches China (1st century CE)
events.summary: Buddhism reached China by the first century CE through contact with India and Central Asia; no single arrival year is known.
events.dateNote: 50 CE is an editorial midpoint for the first century, not an attested arrival year. Precise introduction is unknown; earlier contacts are possible. Retain year 50 only when displayed explicitly as first-century approximation.

events.name: Fall of Han
events.summary: Empire collapses
events.dateNote: 220 marks the end of Eastern Han; long political fragmentation preceded formal abdication.

events.name: Battle of Red Cliffs
events.summary: Sun Quan and Liu Bei's alliance stopped Cao Cao's advance at Red Cliffs during the late Eastern Han.
events.dateNote: 208 CE follows Rafe de Crespigny's scholarly chronology. Winter of Jian'an 13 overlaps 208–209 in Julian conversion. Parent Eastern Han is correct; the formal Three Kingdoms period starts 220.

events.name: Western Jin loses Chang’an
events.summary: Fragmentation begins
events.dateNote: 316 is the fall of Western Jin at Chang’an; Eastern Jin continued in the south.

events.name: Buddhism expands in China (c. 350)
events.summary: Buddhist communities and images spread in divided China during the fourth century.
events.dateNote: 350 is an illustrative midpoint for fourth-century growth, not a dated introduction or single event.

events.name: Reunification
events.summary: Ends division
events.dateNote: 589 marks Sui conquest of Chen and reunification; distinct from Sui foundation in 581.

events.name: An Lushan Rebellion
events.summary: Weakens Tang
events.dateNote: 755 is the onset; the rebellion continued to 763. Keep point at onset; describe 755–763 in summary.

events.name: Expansion of eunuch power in Ming government
events.summary: Eunuchs become major agents of imperial authority
events.dateNote: The exact 1400 marker is unsupported. Proposed circa 1403 is an editorial anchor for expansion under Yongle: accession 1402, reign era 1403–1424. This was a continuing institutional process, not a single decree.

events.name: Wei Zhongxian dominance
events.summary: Eunuch faction dominates late Ming court politics
events.dateNote: 1624 is a supported focal year: Yang Lian's memorial denouncing Wei is dated Tianqi 4. Wei's influence began earlier; major persecutions followed in 1625–1626 and his fall and death in 1627.

events.name: First Opium War
events.summary: Military defeat forces opening to foreign powers
events.dateNote: 1839 is a start-year marker for the 1839–1842 war. It includes initial clashes; some periodizations begin with the main expedition in 1840.

events.name: Taiping Rebellion
events.summary: Massive civil war weakens Qing state
events.dateNote: 1850 is a defensible start for the broader 1850–1864 civil war; 1851 is used for formal uprising/proclamation. Nanjing fell in July 1864; surviving resistance lasted longer.

events.name: Second Opium War
events.summary: Further defeats expand foreign control
events.dateNote: 1856 is the starting marker for the 1856–1860 conflict, which comprised several campaigns and negotiations.

events.name: Self-Strengthening Movement
events.summary: Attempts to modernize military and industry
events.dateNote: Propose circa 1861 as the start anchor, rather than an exact 1860 event. The movement developed from earlier proposals and continued into the 1894–1895 war; scholarly period boundaries vary.

events.name: First Sino-Japanese War
events.summary: Defeat shows failure of reform efforts
events.dateNote: 1894 is the start-year marker for the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895.

events.name: Hundred Days Reform
events.summary: Short-lived reform effort
events.dateNote: 1898 is secure. The reform interval ran June–September; the Palace Museum gives fourth lunar month day 23 through eighth lunar month day 6, 103 days.

events.name: Boxer Rebellion
events.summary: Anti-foreign uprising and intervention
events.dateNote: 1900 is a valid focal marker for the siege and foreign intervention, not the movement's entire duration. Expansion preceded it in 1899 and settlement followed in 1901.

events.name: Xinhai Revolution
events.summary: Leads to end of Qing rule
events.dateNote: 1911 marks the revolutionary outbreak. The republic began in January 1912 and imperial abdication occurred on 12 February 1912.

events.name: Establishment of Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen)
events.summary: Launches market-oriented reform and export economy
events.dateNote: 26 August 1980: approval of Guangdong Special Economic Zone regulations, including Shenzhen. Preparatory policies date to 1979.

events.name: Belt and Road Initiative
events.summary: Expands overseas infrastructure and influence
events.dateNote: The land and maritime initiatives were proposed in September and October 2013. This is the launch year, not the date of every project.

events.name: Xi Jinping assumes party leadership
events.summary: Xi Jinping became Communist Party general secretary in November 2012; he became state president in March 2013.
events.dateNote: 15 November 2012 dates appointment as party general secretary. Political consolidation was a subsequent process, not a completed event that year.

events.name: May Fourth Movement
events.summary: Student-led nationalist and cultural movement
events.dateNote: 4 May 1919 dates the Beijing protest; the wider movement has broader boundaries.

events.name: Long March
events.summary: Communist retreat that reshapes CCP leadership
events.dateNote: 1934 is the beginning anchor. October 1934–October 1936 covers multiple Red Army retreats; 1934–1935 covers the best-known First Front Army route.

events.name: Death of Mao Zedong
events.summary: Ends Mao era and opens path to leadership transition
events.dateNote: Mao died on 9 September 1976.

events.name: Tiananmen protests and crackdown
events.summary: Political crisis in reform-era China
events.dateNote: 1989 covers the protest movement. The Beijing military crackdown occurred on the night of 3–4 June.

events.name: Return of Hong Kong to China
events.summary: Hong Kong sovereignty transfers from Britain to China
events.dateNote: The sovereignty transfer took effect on 1 July 1997. The Joint Declaration was signed in 1984.

events.name: First Chinese crewed space mission
events.summary: Shenzhou 5 makes China the third country to send a human into orbit independently
events.dateNote: Shenzhou 5 launched on 15 October and returned on 16 October 2003.

events.name: Treaty of Chanyuan
events.summary: Establishes stable relations between Song and Liao
events.dateNote: Mid-January 1005 oath exchange follows the winter campaign of 1004; use 1005 in converted Common Era chronology.

events.name: Jingkang Incident
events.summary: Fall of Northern Song to Jin
events.dateNote: 1127 dates Northern Song's fall and imperial captivity, at the culmination of the 1126–1127 crisis.

events.name: Establishment of Southern Song
events.summary: Shift of political center to the south
events.dateNote: 1127 is the conventional beginning of Southern Song following loss of the northern court; do not equate it with the completion of relocation to Hangzhou.

figures.name: Yu the Great (legendary figure)
figures.summary: Legendary flood-control hero and ancestral founder associated with Xia in later Chinese tradition.
figures.dateNote: 2100 BCE is not a verified birth or activity date. No exact lifetime should be assigned. Keep as an undated legendary figure or use a separately labelled editorial placement. Numeric year is retained solely as an editorial placement for compatibility; it is not an asserted historical date.

figures.name: Confucius (traditional birth date)
figures.summary: Teacher and thinker traditionally dated 551–479 BCE; this marker denotes his traditional birth year.
figures.dateNote: 551 BCE is the traditional birth date, not the date his philosophy arose. His traditional lifetime is 551–479 BCE. If figures use lifetime spans, adopt that range consistently.

figures.name: Sun Tzu (traditional c. 500 BCE)
figures.summary: Traditional military sage associated with The Art of War; his life and the text's authorship remain disputed.
figures.dateNote: 500 BCE is only a traditional approximate placement associated with King Helu's reign. Sunzi's historicity and authorship are contested; the surviving Art of War must not be assigned a proven composition date of 500 BCE.

culturalAnchors.name: Terracotta Army (c. 210 BCE)
culturalAnchors.summary: Thousands of terracotta soldiers guarded the First Emperor's burial complex, conventionally dated around 210 BCE.
culturalAnchors.dateNote: Around 210 BCE is a conventional art-historical date associated with the First Emperor's burial. Manufacture occurred over time; this is not a precise creation day/year for every figure.

culturalAnchors.name: Dadu named as the Yuan capital
culturalAnchors.summary: Beijing, already an imperial center, is named Dadu under Kublai Khan.
culturalAnchors.dateNote: 1271 dates adoption of the dynastic name Yuan; 1272 dates the Dadu name and capital milestone. Construction and use as a political center began earlier, so this is not Beijing's first establishment as a capital.

culturalAnchors.name: Beijing confirmed as capital (Yongle)
culturalAnchors.summary: Yongle formally moves the Ming court to Beijing after completion of its palace complex.
culturalAnchors.dateNote: 1420 dates palace completion and preparations; formal transfer occurred in Yongle 19, 1421. Avoid permanent capital, since later governments used other capitals.

culturalAnchors.name: Beijing as Qing capital
culturalAnchors.dateNote: 1644 dates the Qing court's move to Beijing; Qing was proclaimed in 1636, and territorial conquest continued after 1644.

globalContext.name: Alexander the Great
globalContext.summary: Alexander’s conquests dismantled the Achaemenid Persian Empire and extended Macedonian power into Central and South Asia. The 330 BCE marker is an editorial point within those campaigns, not a date for his entire life or all his conquests.
globalContext.dateNote: 330 BCE is a campaign reference, not a biographical date. Keep it only as an explicitly approximate editorial marker. Alexander lived 356–323 BCE; a biographical range is preferable when the display supports ranges.

globalContext.name: Muhammad’s first revelation (traditional date)
globalContext.dateNote: 610 refers to the first revelation in Islamic tradition, not a single date encompassing Islam’s rise.

all.name: Alexander the Great
all.summary: Alexander’s conquests dismantled the Achaemenid Persian Empire and extended Macedonian power into Central and South Asia. The 330 BCE marker is an editorial point within those campaigns, not a date for his entire life or all his conquests.
all.dateNote: 330 BCE is a campaign reference, not a biographical date. Keep it only as an explicitly approximate editorial marker. Alexander lived 356–323 BCE; a biographical range is preferable when the display supports ranges.

all.name: Qin-Han system
all.summary: An umbrella period for Qin and Han imperial rule and their intervening transitions.
all.dateNote: 221 BCE–220 CE is an editorial umbrella for Qin and Han, including intervening conflicts and Xin; not one continuous regime. Stored duration 441 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years are 440 because BCE/CE has no year zero.

all.name: Qin
all.summary: The Qin imperial dynasty followed the conquest of the rival states in 221 BCE.
all.dateNote: 221–206 BCE is the standard museum range for the imperial Qin dynasty, not the longer history of the Qin state.

all.name: Western Han
all.summary: The first phase of Han rule, conventionally dated from Liu Bang's kingship in 206 BCE; he became emperor in 202 BCE.
all.dateNote: 206 BCE–9 CE is the standard museum convention, beginning with Liu Bang's kingship; 202 BCE marks his imperial accession and is used by other historians. Duration 215 is coordinate subtraction; elapsed historical years 214.

all.name: Xin
all.summary: Wang Mang's Xin dynasty interrupted Han rule from 9 to 23 CE.
all.dateNote: 9–23 CE follows the Cambridge History of China chronology for Wang Mang's dynasty.

all.name: Eastern Han
all.summary: The restored Han dynasty, conventionally dated 25–220 CE.
all.dateNote: 25–220 CE follows the Met chronology; restoration in 25 is distinct from the earlier Gengshi claimant 23–25.

all.name: Qin unification
all.summary: Qin completed its conquest of the rival states and established an empire in 221 BCE.
all.dateNote: 221 BCE marks completion of the conquests and formation of imperial Qin.

all.name: Qin standardizes weights and measures
all.summary: Qin's First Emperor ordered a common system of weights and measures across the empire in 221 BCE.
all.dateNote: The specific weights-and-measures edict is dated 221 BCE, not 220. Other standardization measures were a process; narrowing the label provides a defensible single year.

all.name: Han court establishes Five Classics patronage
all.summary: The Han court promoted study of the Five Classics in 136 BCE, an important stage in the growth of state-sponsored classical learning.
all.dateNote: 130 BCE has no specific event support.136 BCE is a documented milestone in official promotion of the Five Classics. Formation of state Confucianism was gradual, not a single adoption event.

all.name: Zhang Qian's first western mission
all.summary: Zhang Qian departed on a western mission conventionally dated 138 BCE, helping expand Han knowledge of Central Asia.
all.dateNote: 130 BCE is unsupported as a precise 'Silk Road expansion' event.138 BCE dates Zhang Qian's departure in the UNESCO education publication; another UNESCO overview uses 139 BCE. Trade routes predated and developed after this mission.

all.name: Buddhism reaches China (1st century CE)
all.summary: Buddhism reached China by the first century CE through contact with India and Central Asia; no single arrival year is known.
all.dateNote: 50 CE is an editorial midpoint for the first century, not an attested arrival year. Precise introduction is unknown; earlier contacts are possible. Retain year 50 only when displayed explicitly as first-century approximation.

all.name: Terracotta Army (c. 210 BCE)
all.summary: Thousands of terracotta soldiers guarded the First Emperor's burial complex, conventionally dated around 210 BCE.
all.dateNote: Around 210 BCE is a conventional art-historical date associated with the First Emperor's burial. Manufacture occurred over time; this is not a precise creation day/year for every figure.

all.name: Three Kingdoms
all.summary: Fragmentation
all.dateNote: 220–280 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Wei
all.summary: Northern state
all.dateNote: 220–265 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Shu
all.summary: Han claimant
all.dateNote: 221–263 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Wu
all.summary: Southern state
all.dateNote: 222–280 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Fall of Han
all.summary: Empire collapses
all.dateNote: 220 marks the end of Eastern Han; long political fragmentation preceded formal abdication.

all.name: Battle of Red Cliffs
all.summary: Sun Quan and Liu Bei's alliance stopped Cao Cao's advance at Red Cliffs during the late Eastern Han.
all.dateNote: 208 CE follows Rafe de Crespigny's scholarly chronology. Winter of Jian'an 13 overlaps 208–209 in Julian conversion. Parent Eastern Han is correct; the formal Three Kingdoms period starts 220.

all.name: Western Jin
all.summary: Short reunification
all.dateNote: 266–316 is supported with calendrical qualification: Cambridge explicitly gives 265 or 266 for the foundation. Retain 266.

all.name: Western Jin loses Chang’an
all.summary: Fragmentation begins
all.dateNote: 316 is the fall of Western Jin at Chang’an; Eastern Jin continued in the south.

all.name: Buddhism expands in China (c. 350)
all.summary: Buddhist communities and images spread in divided China during the fourth century.
all.dateNote: 350 is an illustrative midpoint for fourth-century growth, not a dated introduction or single event.

all.name: Sui-Tang
all.summary: Reunification
all.dateNote: 581–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

all.name: Sui
all.summary: Reunifies China
all.dateNote: 581–618 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

all.name: Tang
all.summary: Imperial peak
all.dateNote: 618–907 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

all.name: Reunification
all.summary: Ends division
all.dateNote: 589 marks Sui conquest of Chen and reunification; distinct from Sui foundation in 581.

all.name: An Lushan Rebellion
all.summary: Weakens Tang
all.dateNote: 755 is the onset; the rebellion continued to 763. Keep point at onset; describe 755–763 in summary.

all.name: Muhammad’s first revelation (traditional date)
all.summary: New civilization
all.dateNote: 610 refers to the first revelation in Islamic tradition, not a single date encompassing Islam’s rise.

all.name: Dadu named as the Yuan capital
all.summary: Beijing, already an imperial center, is named Dadu under Kublai Khan.
all.dateNote: 1271 dates adoption of the dynastic name Yuan; 1272 dates the Dadu name and capital milestone. Construction and use as a political center began earlier, so this is not Beijing's first establishment as a capital.

all.name: Beijing confirmed as capital (Yongle)
all.summary: Yongle formally moves the Ming court to Beijing after completion of its palace complex.
all.dateNote: 1420 dates palace completion and preparations; formal transfer occurred in Yongle 19, 1421. Avoid permanent capital, since later governments used other capitals.

all.name: Beijing as Qing capital
all.summary: Continues as imperial center
all.dateNote: 1644 dates the Qing court's move to Beijing; Qing was proclaimed in 1636, and territorial conquest continued after 1644.

all.name: Expansion of eunuch power in Ming government
all.summary: Eunuchs become major agents of imperial authority
all.dateNote: The exact 1400 marker is unsupported. Proposed circa 1403 is an editorial anchor for expansion under Yongle: accession 1402, reign era 1403–1424. This was a continuing institutional process, not a single decree.

all.name: Wei Zhongxian dominance
all.summary: Eunuch faction dominates late Ming court politics
all.dateNote: 1624 is a supported focal year: Yang Lian's memorial denouncing Wei is dated Tianqi 4. Wei's influence began earlier; major persecutions followed in 1625–1626 and his fall and death in 1627.

all.name: First Opium War
all.summary: Military defeat forces opening to foreign powers
all.dateNote: 1839 is a start-year marker for the 1839–1842 war. It includes initial clashes; some periodizations begin with the main expedition in 1840.

all.name: Taiping Rebellion
all.summary: Massive civil war weakens Qing state
all.dateNote: 1850 is a defensible start for the broader 1850–1864 civil war; 1851 is used for formal uprising/proclamation. Nanjing fell in July 1864; surviving resistance lasted longer.

all.name: Second Opium War
all.summary: Further defeats expand foreign control
all.dateNote: 1856 is the starting marker for the 1856–1860 conflict, which comprised several campaigns and negotiations.

all.name: Self-Strengthening Movement
all.summary: Attempts to modernize military and industry
all.dateNote: Propose circa 1861 as the start anchor, rather than an exact 1860 event. The movement developed from earlier proposals and continued into the 1894–1895 war; scholarly period boundaries vary.

all.name: First Sino-Japanese War
all.summary: Defeat shows failure of reform efforts
all.dateNote: 1894 is the start-year marker for the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895.

all.name: Hundred Days Reform
all.summary: Short-lived reform effort
all.dateNote: 1898 is secure. The reform interval ran June–September; the Palace Museum gives fourth lunar month day 23 through eighth lunar month day 6, 103 days.

all.name: Boxer Rebellion
all.summary: Anti-foreign uprising and intervention
all.dateNote: 1900 is a valid focal marker for the siege and foreign intervention, not the movement's entire duration. Expansion preceded it in 1899 and settlement followed in 1901.

all.name: Xinhai Revolution
all.summary: Leads to end of Qing rule
all.dateNote: 1911 marks the revolutionary outbreak. The republic began in January 1912 and imperial abdication occurred on 12 February 1912.

all.name: Establishment of Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen)
all.summary: Launches market-oriented reform and export economy
all.dateNote: 26 August 1980: approval of Guangdong Special Economic Zone regulations, including Shenzhen. Preparatory policies date to 1979.

all.name: Belt and Road Initiative
all.summary: Expands overseas infrastructure and influence
all.dateNote: The land and maritime initiatives were proposed in September and October 2013. This is the launch year, not the date of every project.

all.name: Xi Jinping assumes party leadership
all.summary: Xi Jinping became Communist Party general secretary in November 2012; he became state president in March 2013.
all.dateNote: 15 November 2012 dates appointment as party general secretary. Political consolidation was a subsequent process, not a completed event that year.

all.name: Modern China
all.summary: Republican, revolutionary, and state-building era
all.dateNote: 1912–2026 is an editorial exhibition frame. Modern China has no universally agreed beginning; 2026 is a display horizon.

all.name: Republic of China (mainland period)
all.summary: Republican state on mainland China before 1949
all.dateNote: 1 January 1912 is the republic’s founding. 1949 ends this mainland-period card, not the existence of the ROC government, which relocated to Taiwan. Qing abdication followed on 12 February 1912.

all.name: People's Republic of China
all.summary: Modern Chinese state founded in 1949
all.dateNote: Proclaimed 1 October 1949. 2026 is the dataset display horizon, not an end date.

all.name: May Fourth Movement
all.summary: Student-led nationalist and cultural movement
all.dateNote: 4 May 1919 dates the Beijing protest; the wider movement has broader boundaries.

all.name: Long March
all.summary: Communist retreat that reshapes CCP leadership
all.dateNote: 1934 is the beginning anchor. October 1934–October 1936 covers multiple Red Army retreats; 1934–1935 covers the best-known First Front Army route.

all.name: Death of Mao Zedong
all.summary: Ends Mao era and opens path to leadership transition
all.dateNote: Mao died on 9 September 1976.

all.name: Tiananmen protests and crackdown
all.summary: Political crisis in reform-era China
all.dateNote: 1989 covers the protest movement. The Beijing military crackdown occurred on the night of 3–4 June.

all.name: Return of Hong Kong to China
all.summary: Hong Kong sovereignty transfers from Britain to China
all.dateNote: The sovereignty transfer took effect on 1 July 1997. The Joint Declaration was signed in 1984.

all.name: First Chinese crewed space mission
all.summary: Shenzhou 5 makes China the third country to send a human into orbit independently
all.dateNote: Shenzhou 5 launched on 15 October and returned on 16 October 2003.

all.name: Song multi-state system
all.summary: Multi-state balance between Song, Liao, Jin, and Western Xia
all.dateNote: 960–1279 follows the Song dynasty as an editorial frame for changing concurrent states. The named states did not all coexist throughout the interval, and this aggregate does not assert Song sovereignty over them.

all.name: Northern Song
all.summary: Reunifies much of China
all.dateNote: 960–1127 is the standard Northern Song chronology.

all.name: Southern Song
all.summary: Southern continuation after loss of north
all.dateNote: 1127–1279 is the standard Southern Song chronology; 1127 does not mean the court immediately settled permanently at Hangzhou.

all.name: Liao (Khitan)
all.summary: Steppe empire controlling north China
all.dateNote: 907–1125 is a supported Khitan-state convention; 916 denotes imperial proclamation. Name already qualifies Liao as Khitan.

all.name: Western Xia
all.summary: Tangut state in northwest
all.dateNote: 1038 dates imperial proclamation by Li Yuanhao; Tangut power predates it. UNESCO's reviewed chronology supports 1038–1227.

all.name: Jin (Jurchen)
all.summary: Conquers northern Song and dominates north China
all.dateNote: 1115–1234 dates the Jurchen Jin; distinct from the earlier Jin (晋).

all.name: Treaty of Chanyuan
all.summary: Establishes stable relations between Song and Liao
all.dateNote: Mid-January 1005 oath exchange follows the winter campaign of 1004; use 1005 in converted Common Era chronology.

all.name: Jingkang Incident
all.summary: Fall of Northern Song to Jin
all.dateNote: 1127 dates Northern Song's fall and imperial captivity, at the culmination of the 1126–1127 crisis.

all.name: Establishment of Southern Song
all.summary: Shift of political center to the south
all.dateNote: 1127 is the conventional beginning of Southern Song following loss of the northern court; do not equate it with the completion of relocation to Hangzhou.

all.name: Yuan
all.summary: Mongol dynasty ruling China
all.dateNote: 1271 dates the Yuan dynastic name, 1279 the final Song conquest. 1368 ends Yuan rule from Beijing, not all subsequent Mongol or Northern Yuan rule.

all.name: Ming
all.summary: Restoration of Han Chinese rule after Yuan
all.dateNote: 1368–1644 is the main Ming court convention. Southern Ming successors survived after Beijing fell.

all.name: Qing
all.summary: Manchu dynasty ruling a multiethnic empire
all.dateNote: 1644–1912 is valid for rule from Beijing. The Qing dynastic name was proclaimed in 1636; the emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, after the revolution began in 1911.

all.name: Eastern Jin
all.summary: The Jin court continued in southern China at Jiankang after losing the north, alongside rival northern states.
all.dateNote: 317–420 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Han Zhao (Former Zhao)
all.summary: Founded as Han, this state later adopted the name Zhao; its armies captured the Western Jin capitals.
all.dateNote: 304–329 includes the Han phase; Former Zhao naming begins 319. Retain combined label.

all.name: Later Zhao
all.summary: Shi Le founded a rival Zhao state that became a major power in northern China.
all.dateNote: Cambridge History table confirms 319–351; EMC thesaurus gives a different 352 endpoint.

all.name: Former Yan
all.summary: The Murong Xianbei founded this northern state, which expanded into the Central Plain before conquest by Former Qin.
all.dateNote: 337–370 is the China Institute/Liaoning archaeology exhibition chronology; 337 is royal proclamation.

all.name: Former Qin
all.summary: Former Qin briefly unified northern China; defeat by Eastern Jin at the Fei River in 383 precipitated its fragmentation.
all.dateNote: 351–394 agrees with EMC scholarly thesaurus. Other tables differ; retain conventional terminal remnant date.

all.name: Later Qin
all.summary: A Qiang-led state based at Chang'an, Later Qin supported Buddhist translation before conquest by Eastern Jin.
all.dateNote: 384–417 agrees with scholarly thesaurus.

all.name: Liu Song
all.summary: Liu Yu replaced Eastern Jin, founding the first of the four Southern Dynasties.
all.dateNote: 420–479 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Southern Qi
all.summary: The Xiao family's short-lived dynasty succeeded Liu Song in southern China.
all.dateNote: 479–502 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Liang
all.summary: A southern dynasty based at Jiankang, remembered for court culture and Buddhist patronage.
all.dateNote: 502–557 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Chen
all.summary: The last Southern Dynasty ruled from Jiankang until Sui conquered it in 589.
all.dateNote: 557–589 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Northern Wei
all.summary: Founded by the Tuoba Xianbei, Northern Wei unified the north in 439 before dividing into eastern and western successors.
all.dateNote: 386–534 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Eastern Wei
all.summary: The eastern successor to Northern Wei governed from Ye before replacement by Northern Qi.
all.dateNote: 534–550 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Western Wei
all.summary: The western successor to Northern Wei ruled from Chang'an before Northern Zhou replaced it.
all.dateNote: 535–557 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Northern Qi
all.summary: Northern Qi succeeded Eastern Wei and competed with Northern Zhou, which conquered it in 577.
all.dateNote: 550–577 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Northern Zhou
all.summary: Northern Zhou replaced Western Wei, conquered Northern Qi in 577, and gave way to Sui in 581.
all.dateNote: 557–581 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Later Liang
all.summary: Zhu Wen replaced Tang with Later Liang, the first of five successive northern dynasties.
all.dateNote: 907–923 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

all.name: Later Tang
all.summary: Li Cunxu established this Shatuo-led dynasty after overthrowing Later Liang.
all.dateNote: 923–936 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

all.name: Later Jin
all.summary: Shi Jingtang founded Later Jin with Khitan support; a later Khitan invasion ended the dynasty.
all.dateNote: Cambridge journal explicitly supports the existing endpoints; older tables give one-year-earlier terminal years.

all.name: Later Han
all.summary: Liu Zhiyuan founded this short-lived northern dynasty after the fall of Later Jin.
all.dateNote: Cambridge journal explicitly supports the existing endpoints; older tables give one-year-earlier terminal years.

all.name: Later Zhou
all.summary: The last of the Five Dynasties strengthened the northern state before Zhao Kuangyin founded Song.
all.dateNote: 951–960 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

all.name: Wu (Yang Wu)
all.summary: Based in the lower Yangtze region, Wu grew from late-Tang regional rule and was replaced by Southern Tang.
all.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

all.name: Former Shu
all.summary: Wang Jian founded an independent state in Sichuan; Later Tang conquered it in 925.
all.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

all.name: Wuyue
all.summary: The Qian family's coastal kingdom in the Zhejiang region endured until its submission to Song in 978.
all.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

all.name: Chu (Ma Chu)
all.summary: The Ma family ruled this Hunan-based kingdom until Southern Tang intervention ended the dynasty.
all.dateNote: 907–951 is supported by Kurz; 927 is the later kingdom milestone used in other tables. Retain broad state span.

all.name: Min
all.summary: The Wang family's Fujian-based kingdom fragmented through internal conflict before its collapse.
all.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

all.name: Southern Han
all.summary: Based at Guangzhou, this southern kingdom was founded as Yue and renamed Han before eventual Song conquest.
all.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

all.name: Jingnan (Nanping)
all.summary: A small kingdom around Jingzhou on the middle Yangtze, Jingnan survived between larger neighbors until Song conquest.
all.dateNote: Existing range confirmed by Cambridge History of China, volume 5 introduction table; starts use state-formation milestones.

all.name: Later Shu
all.summary: The Meng family restored an independent Sichuan kingdom after Former Shu; Song conquered it in 965.
all.dateNote: 934–965 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

all.name: Southern Tang
all.summary: Southern Tang replaced Wu in the lower Yangtze and fostered an influential court culture before Song conquest.
all.dateNote: 937–975 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

all.name: Northern Han
all.summary: Based at Taiyuan, this northern member of the Ten Kingdoms survived with Khitan support until Song conquered it.
all.dateNote: 951–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

all.name: Sixteen Kingdoms
all.summary: A period of rival states, chiefly in northern China, alongside the Jin courts; Northern Wei unified the north in 439.
all.dateNote: 304–439 follows the museum chronology.

all.name: Northern and Southern Dynasties
all.summary: Successive southern courts and rival northern dynasties coexisted until Sui conquered Chen in 589.
all.dateNote: 420–589 is a supported periodization; Northern Wei began earlier, in 386. Do not infer containment of all northern states.

all.name: Five Dynasties
all.summary: Five successive dynasties held the northern imperial succession between Tang and Song.
all.dateNote: 907–960 is supported; Sui–Tang is an editorial aggregate, not one dynasty.

all.name: Ten Kingdoms
all.summary: Regional states coexisted with the Five Dynasties and early Song, with Northern Han the last to fall in 979.
all.dateNote: 902–979 agrees with Jordan's university-hosted reign table.

meta.dateAuditScope: All 111 record date fields; source conventions and uncertainty recorded per row.
